A Colorado couple who had been together for 15 years tied the knot inside a hospital just days before the bride underwent major brain tumour surgery, after nurses and caregivers organised an entire wedding in less than 24 hours.Gary Clayson proposed to his longtime partner, Anne, on July 23 at AdventHealth Porter in Denver after learning she was scheduled for intensive surgery to remove a large brain tumour. Determined to make their relationship official before the operation, Gary asked the hospital staff to help arrange a wedding the very next day."Yeah, she's the last person I'm going to be with. So, we're going to make it official," Gary told local outlet 9News.With less than a day's notice, nurses and hospital staff quickly came together to turn the couple's wish into reality."We were the wedding planning party. So, we had someone working on the cake, someone working on the photographer," nurse Breanne Burley told 9News.According to AdventHealth Porter, caregivers from across the hospital coordinated every aspect of the celebration. They arranged Anne's favourite flowers, decorated the aisle with candles, organised a photographer and videographer, provided a wedding cake and sparkling cider, and even helped the bride with her makeup and dress on the morning of the ceremony."When our team learned that Anne and Gary Clayson hoped to be married before Anne underwent brain surgery, caregivers from across the hospital came together in less than 24 hours to make that wish a reality," a hospital spokesperson said in a statement to People.A video from the ceremony captured an emotional Gary waiting for Anne as she walked down the aisle inside the hospital."There she is, my beautiful bride," he said, adding, "Anne, you look beautiful, you look really nice."During their vows, Anne told guests that they would celebrate again after her surgery."On Monday is the DJ and you guys will all be there with us when they remove the tumour," she said. "This guy has been taking care of me. We've been through a lot."Asked what he loved most about Anne, Gary simply replied, "Everything," adding that she was "perfect."The couple exchanged rings and sealed their vows with a kiss before Anne underwent surgery on July 27.Breanne Burley, Chief Nursing Officer at AdventHealth Porter, said the effort reflected the hospital's commitment to compassionate care."When our team came together to turn a proposal into a wedding in less than 24 hours, just before life-changing brain surgery, it reflected AdventHealth Porter's mission and culture at the core," Burley told People."It gave this couple hope in the midst of uncertainty, love through compassion and a reminder that every patient is a person beyond their diagnosis," she said, adding that the caregivers were honoured to help Anne and Gary begin married life surrounded by the hospital team that had become "like family" during her treatment.
Article Summary: Gary Clayson proposed to his longtime partner, Anne, on July 23 at AdventHealth Porter in Denver. Determined to make their relationship official before the operation, Gary asked the hospital staff to help arrange a wedding the very next day. With less than a day's notice, nurses and hospital staff quickly came together to turn the couple's wish into reality.

Article Title: Burnt-out vehicles, rock-strewn roads, heavy security: PoK votes in second phase amid unrest
Article Text:
The elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (PoK) have been overshadowed by violence, allegations of electoral rigging and reports of enforced disappearances



Heavy security, protests overshadow polling

India rejects PoK polls

Pakistan conducted the second phase of legislative assembly elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) on Sunday amid fresh unrest, with residents reporting burnt vehicles, rock-strewn roads and heavy security across parts of Muzaffarabad following clashes between protesters and security forces.The voting is taking place in the second of three phases for the 45 directly elected seats of the 53-member assembly. However, the polls have been overshadowed by nearly two months of protests, allegations of election irregularities, political boycotts and a security crackdown.Residents of Muzaffarabad said fresh violence ahead of polling had raised concerns that the unrest would dominate the election process. Local reports described burnt-out vehicles, roads blocked with rocks and a strong presence of police, paramilitary personnel and army troops in several areas after clashes between demonstrators and security forces.Pakistan has deployed a three-tier security arrangement across PoK, with police, Pakistan Rangers, the Federal Constabulary and around 2,100 army personnel guarding polling stations.The elections come against the backdrop of sustained protests led by the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), which has been demanding greater political freedoms, economic reforms and the abolition of 12 assembly seats reserved for Pakistan-based refugees.The group has also sought better healthcare, education, employment opportunities and reduced political privileges.JAAC has boycotted the elections, arguing that the reserved refugee seats allow Pakistan's mainstream political parties to influence government formation in the region.The protest movement has intensified in recent weeks after talks with the authorities collapsed, leading to large demonstrations, strikes and clashes. Polling in two constituencies was postponed because of the deteriorating security situation.Rights groups, including the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, the United Nations and Amnesty International, have criticised the crackdown on protesters, internet restrictions and the ban imposed on JAAC under anti-terrorism laws.India has rejected the elections, describing them as a 'cosmetic' exercise aimed at legitimising Pakistan's 'illegal occupation' of the region.External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the entire Union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, including areas under Pakistan's control are an integral part of India.He said the elections were an attempt by Pakistan to 'camouflage its illegal occupation' and conceal alleged human rights violations in the region."The current cosmetic electoral exercise is nothing but an attempt by Pakistan to camouflage its illegal occupation and hide its grave human rights violations in the region. The ongoing mass protest in the Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir is the direct consequence of its economic exploitation, its denial of fundamental rights to the people and its administrative oppression," Jaiswal had said earlier this week.
Article Summary: Pakistan conducted the second phase of legislative assembly elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoK) on Sunday. Residents reported burnt vehicles, rock-strewn roads and heavy security across parts of Muzaffarabad. The voting is taking place in the second of three phases for the 45 directly elected seats of the 53-member assembly. The polls have been overshadowed by nearly two months of protests, allegations of election irregularities, political boycotts and a security crackdown.

Article Title: ‘Dhurandhar’ gangster’s brother shot in Karachi
Article Text:
Personal enmity or gang war? Probe on into hit on Zubair Baloch

Zubair Baloch — the brother of jailed Pakistan gangster Uzair Baloch, whose ruthless ascent was dramatised in the movie ‘Dhurandhar’ — is learned to be critically wounded following a targeted drive-by shooting in Karachi’s Lyari neighbourhood on Thursday evening, reports .The 40-year-old was sitting outside his Singu Lane home when two masked assailants on a motorcycle opened fire, striking him in the chest and abdomen.Zubair was rushed to Civil Hospital Karachi for emergency surgery. Two bystanders were also injured in the crossfire, with one reported to be in serious condition.According to Pakistan police, the attackers fled after a nearby shopkeeper returned fire. CCTV footage from the spot, which surfaced on Telegram channels, showed chaos on the street as the gunmen escaped.Police told the local press they were probing angles of personal enmity and the potential resurgence of long-standing gang wars.Zubair, arrested in multiple criminal cases in 2012, was released from prison last year, while his brother Uzair remains in jail serving a 12-year sentence handed down by a military court.Uzair and several accomplices were indicted for a 2012 armed attack on law enforcement officers under Kalakot police station’s jurisdiction.In April 2020, Uzair Baloch received a 12-year prison sentence for espionage.For decades, the historic Karachi neighbourhood of Lyari served as the epicentre of a gang war and a hub of organised crime. The turmoil traces back to early turf battles over drug trade routes and extortion rackets, which eventually expanded into a high-stakes proxy war involving major political factions.Notorious figures such as Sardar Abdul Rehman Baloch aka Rehman Dakait and his fierce rival Arshad Pappu turned narrow alleyways into battlegrounds, leveraging strategic political patronage through outfits like Peoples’ Aman Committee to insulate their syndicates from police oversight. Following Rehman Dakait’s death in a 2009 police encounter, his cousin Uzair Baloch stepped in to control the dominant faction.
Article Summary: Zubair Baloch, 40, was shot in the chest and abdomen on Thursday evening. He was sitting outside his home when two masked assailants opened fire. Two bystanders were also injured in the crossfire, with one reported to be in serious condition. Police are probing angles of personal enmity and the potential resurgence of gang wars.

Article Title: Pakistan minister invokes 'cockroaches' analogy, says united Gen-Z can 'turn everything upside down'
Article Text:
Calls for new provinces and decentralisation

'Biggest supporter' of democracy

Youth want jobs, not handouts

'Cockroaches' remark

Business community urged to back reforms

Mounting debt concerns

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for the youth? Merit-based jobs Welfare schemes Internships and training programs 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi on Thursday declared that the country's governance system had "collapsed", calling for the creation of new administrative units or provinces and urging political parties to reach a consensus on sweeping constitutional and governance reforms. He warned that without structural changes, Pakistan would remain trapped in recurring political and economic crises.Addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit 2026 in Islamabad, Naqvi said Pakistan's decades-old governance model had failed to deliver justice, economic opportunities or effective public services. He argued that decentralisation and the emergence of new leadership were essential to reform the country."Whether you agree or not, the system we have been living under has collapsed."Naqvi said repeated attempts to fix Pakistan's problems within the existing framework had failed, adding that the same debates would continue even a decade later unless the country's governance structure was fundamentally reformed."I believe the people responsible for bringing Pakistan to its current state are sitting in this hall," he said, adding that if a system had failed to function effectively for 70 to 80 years, there must be fundamental flaws in its design.The interior minister said the solution lay in decentralising governance through the creation of additional administrative units or provinces, arguing that local ownership would improve governance and allow new political leadership to emerge."The solution is only one.""You will have to take [the matter of] administrative units, provinces or whatever you may call it, to the public.""Unless units are made and they take ownership, and a new leadership comes, this will not happen."Naqvi urged all political parties to negotiate a comprehensive reform agenda instead of continuing with what he described as an outdated governance structure."All political parties should sit together in a single room, whether for a day, a month or a year. They will have to settle every issue of their country, including new units and provinces.""Unless they do so, unless they sit together and change this, this country will remain in the same condition, regardless of how many seminars and functions you hold."While describing himself as "the biggest supporter" of democracy, Naqvi argued that democratic governance could take different institutional forms and said Pakistan should not remain tied to a system that had consistently underperformed."We all want democracy. I am the biggest supporter of democracy and will remain so. But there are five or six systems within democracy. Yet we insist that no matter what happens, we must continue dragging along the same one."He also criticised policy failures, saying Pakistan continued to import agricultural commodities such as wheat despite being an agricultural country.Naqvi acknowledged the long working hours of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif but argued that the government remained focused on crisis management instead of long-term reforms."I have seen Shehbaz Sharif work 12 to 14 hours a day. He could even work 18 hours a day, but we are only firefighting.""Until you correct the basics of this country while adhering to the spirit of democracy, this will remain the same."Naqvi said Pakistan's young people were demanding merit-based employment, transparent recruitment and equal opportunities rather than welfare schemes or financial assistance."We think giving youngsters stipends of a few thousand rupees a month or tablets will make them happy, but ask them what they really want.""Their only demand is merit-based jobs and employment opportunities. They are not asking you for tablets or a few thousand rupees every month."According to the minister, Pakistani youth had the potential to earn between $2,000 and $4,000 per month if provided with the right opportunities.Referring to a term that has recently been used for Gen-Z in the wake of student protests in India, Naqvi warned that growing frustration among young people should not be ignored."If these 'Cockroaches' get united, they can turn everything upside down."He said the government should address the aspirations of young people before dissatisfaction intensified, arguing that their primary demands centred on merit-based jobs and equal opportunities.Naqvi also called on Pakistan's business community to play a more active role in reforming the country's political system, arguing that industrialists and traders had long been intertwined with politics."One gives funding of Rs500 million before elections, or the other gives Rs100 million or Rs50 million."He questioned why business leaders preferred financing political candidates instead of contesting elections themselves."Why don't businessmen enter politics? You are willing to fund politicians, but consider entering politics yourselves to be something shameful. You will have to stand up for yourselves."Highlighting Pakistan's fiscal challenges, Naqvi likened the federal government's finances to a household beginning every month already burdened with debt."The condition of this federal government is such that we make our budgets in the negative, and we discuss how much debt we have to incur this year.""[...] We will take more debts, but we will not correct things."He said leaders across the political spectrum understood the country's structural problems but had repeatedly failed to implement reforms, urging all stakeholders to build consensus on a long-term governance overhaul.
Article Summary: Mohsin Naqvi says Pakistan's governance system has "collapsed" Calls for creation of new administrative units or provinces. Urges political parties to reach consensus on constitutional and governance reforms. Calls on business community to play more active role in reforming the country.

Article Title: 34 killed as methane explosion tears through coal mine in Pakistan's Balochistan
Article Text:
Coal mine blast in Pakistan's Balochistan (AP photo)

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think the compensation offered to families of miners is sufficient? Yes, it's fair No, it’s inadequate 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

At least 34 miners in Pakistan were killed and 10 other remained trapped after a methane gas explosion ripped through a coal mine in Balochistan province on Thursday, as officials told news agency AP.While rescuers continued a race against time to reach those still underground.The explosion took place on the outskirts of Quetta, the provincial capital, and was apparently triggered by a buildup of methane gas, according to government mine inspector Ghani Baloch.Rescue teams initially recovered the bodies of seven miners before locating 25 more, provincial officials and the disaster management agency said in a statement. The search and rescue operation was continuing as teams worked to locate and recover the remaining trapped workers.Baloch said rescue efforts would continue until all those trapped were accounted for, but warned that the death toll was likely to rise.“The chances of finding anyone alive diminish after methane gas explosions because oxygen levels drop to zero, and rescuers are also proceeding cautiously inside the mine,” Baloch said.Authorities have begun handing over the recovered bodies to their families for burial, while relatives of the missing miners continued to wait anxiously for updates, Baloch added.Balochistan's minister for mines and minerals Shoaib Nosherwani said rescue personnel were operating under extremely challenging conditions.Nosherwani expressed condolences to the victims' families and announced that the provincial government would provide compensation of 500,000 Pakistani rupees (about $1,800) to the family of each miner killed in the blast.He said authorities would conduct a thorough investigation into the cause of the explosion and review mining safety measures to prevent similar incidents.Meanwhile, the Pakistan Central Mines Labour Federation alleged that negligence may have contributed to the disaster. In a statement, the union urged the government to strictly enforce mining safety regulations and take stringent action against companies that violate mine safety laws.Fatal accidents are frequent in Pakistan's coal mining industry, particularly in Balochistan, where many mines operate without adequate ventilation, gas monitoring systems or other essential safety measures.Labour groups and mine workers have repeatedly accused mine owners of ignoring safety standards and failing to provide proper protective equipment.Despite the hazardous working conditions and meagre wages, thousands of people continue to rely on coal mining for their livelihoods in Balochistan, Pakistan's largest yet least developed province, where poverty and unemployment remain widespread.
Article Summary: The explosion took place on the outskirts of Quetta, the provincial capital, and was apparently triggered by a buildup of methane gas. Rescue teams initially recovered the bodies of seven miners before locating 25 more. The search and rescue operation was continuing as teams worked to locate and recover the remaining trapped workers.

Article Title: 11 police personnel, 15 militants killed in overnight attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (ANI file photo)

Pakistan suffered a major overnight militant attack on a police post in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, leaving 11 police personnel and 15 attackers dead by early Thursday.The attack targeted the Khazina police post in Hangu district, close to the Afghanistan border. Responding security forces fought back, killing 15 militants during the exchange of fire, police official Irfan Khan said.No group immediately claimed responsibility for the assault, though suspicion is expected to fall on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has intensified attacks on Pakistani security forces in the border region in recent months.The dead included police officer Diyar Khan, who was leading a reinforcement team to the attacked outpost, according to a statement from the provincial police. More than two dozen police personnel were also injured in the fighting.Police said the militants used heavy weapons to storm the post. Reinforcements heading to the scene were ambushed on the way, with an armoured personnel carrier damaged before officers regrouped and engaged the attackers, eventually forcing them back.Pakistan has seen a steady rise in militant violence in recent years, with the TTP blamed for many of the attacks. Although the group is separate from Afghanistan's ruling Taliban. Since the Taliban returned to power in Kabul in 2021, Islamabad has repeatedly accused the Afghan government of sheltering TTP militants, a charge that Kabul has consistently denied.
Article Summary: Attack targeted Khazina police post in Hangu district, close to the Afghanistan border. Responding security forces fought back, killing 15 militants during the exchange of fire. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the assault, though suspicion is expected to fall on the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)

Article Title: 'Frustration of their failure': Ex-envoy Vidya Bhushan Soni slams Pakistan over PoK unrest
Article Text:
Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (ANI file photo)

NEW DELHI: As unrest intensified in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) during the region's ongoing elections, former Indian envoy to Ukraine Vidya Bhushan Soni said the protests reflected growing frustration among people over Pakistan's failure to address its economic and domestic challenges.His remarks came after Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif called people in PoK as "enemies like India".Speaking to news agency ANI, Soni said frustration was growing in Pakistan because the country had expected to benefit by projecting itself as a mediator in international affairs and hoped that would help it secure economic assistance. "I think again there is a frustration creeping in, in Pakistan. Because they thought that they were playing the mediator role and they thought things would be fine and they would be once again back into business in terms of getting some economic aid, etc. That's not happening," he said.Soni said several groups opposed to the Pakistani government, including Baloch groups and people in PoK, were now putting pressure on Islamabad because they believed the country had reached a difficult position. According to him, Pakistan was more focused on projecting itself internationally as a peaceful nation than solving the problems of its own people."They are the ones who feel that we must put the pressure because now Pakistan is pushed to the wall.And so that's why they are coming out on the street; they are showing their frustration, they're showing their anger, they're showing their patience is running thin," he said.He added that Pakistan should first address the concerns of its own citizens instead of trying to play a larger role on the global stage. "You have to do something about the people, their own people, rather than trying to go and solve the world's problem; first you solve your own problem back home," Soni said.Warning that the unrest was unlikely to end anytime soon, Soni alleged that Pakistan could respond by using force against its own people because its priorities remained focused on international issues. "It has consequences; it will not stop because Pakistan's priority still continues to be international, and they will try to come down heavily through the use of force on their own people," he said.Calling the situation in PoK particularly worrying, Soni said many residents felt their grievances were being ignored, which had deepened their frustration. "The worrisome factor right now is POK because they have seen that their case is not being heard; they are totally ignored. So I feel that it's a frustration of their failure," he said.Meanwhile, the Jammu Kashmir Joint Awami Action Committee (JKAAC), through a series of posts on X, raised concerns over the treatment of injured people and the presence of masked individuals in civilian clothing alongside police personnel during the crackdown. "The treatment of the injured and the presence of masked individuals in civilian clothing alongside police officers raise serious concerns that require urgent scrutiny," the group said.The committee also alleged that civilian property had been damaged during the operation, saying, "The destruction of civilian property raises serious concerns about the conduct of the security forces during the ongoing crackdown." It further claimed that surveillance equipment had been deliberately destroyed, adding, "The deliberate destruction of surveillance equipment raises serious concerns about transparency, accountability, and the preservation of evidence. "Calling for international attention, the JKAAC urged the United Nations, international media, diplomatic missions and human rights organisations to examine the footage from the clashes and launch an independent probe. "We call on the United Nations, international media, diplomatic missions, and international human rights organisations to examine this footage, independently verify the facts, and support an immediate, independent and impartial international investigation into the recent events in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir," the group said.
Article Summary: Former Indian envoy to Ukraine Vidya Bhushan Soni says protests reflect Pakistan's failure to address its economic and domestic challenges. Soni said frustration was growing in Pakistan because the country had expected to benefit by projecting itself as a mediator in international affairs. Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif called people in PoK as "enemies like India"

Article Title: Is Pakistan facilitating Chinese missile shipments to Iran? Islamabad responds
Article Text:
Pakistan army chief Asim Munir (AP file photo)

Pakistan has pushed back strongly against reports claiming it would act as a conduit for Chinese-made weapons headed to Iran, as Tehran remains locked in a tense standoff with the Donald Trump-led US administration.The rejection by Munir's military comes as Islamabad continues its familiar balancing act, staying aligned with China while courting Trump-led Washington, exposing its two-faced tendency in its foreign policy approach.Pakistan’s military chief has recently found favour with US President Donald Trump , while Islamabad continues to project itself as a potential bridge between its neighbour Iran and the United States.Reacting to reports that Pakistan was set to facilitate the transit of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air defence missile systems to Iran, the Trump's "favourite field marshal"-led army dismissed the claims outright.“All such speculations are baseless and devoid of truth,” Pakistan’s military media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), said, according to Azerbaijan news, citing Anadolu Agency.“Such speculations are categorically rejected,” the ISPR added.The denial came after Reuters reported on Wednesday that Iran was expected to receive its first shipment of Chinese air defence systems within weeks, as Tehran looks to rebuild its defensive capabilities amid its conflict with the United States.According to Reuters, the initial deliveries were planned to move from Urumqi in western China and pass through Pakistan before reaching Iran, citing unnamed sources familiar with the matter. The sources, however, did not clarify whether the transit would take place by air or through land routes.The reports emerged amid speculation over US weapons stockpiles being stretched due to ongoing global conflicts, though Trump later dismissed such concerns. The episode has once again highlighted Islamabad’s delicate balancing act between Beijing and Washington as tensions continue to rise around Iran.
Article Summary: Pakistan denies reports it would act as a conduit for Chinese-made weapons headed to Iran. Comes as Islamabad continues its familiar balancing act, staying aligned with China while courting Trump-led Washington. Islamabad continues to project itself as a potential bridge between its neighbour Iran and the United States.

Article Title: Security forces’ crackdown, civil unrest continue in POK, 20 dead
Article Text:
File photo: PoK unrest

The situation in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir ( POK ) remains volatile amid mass civilian unrest, election-related violence, and heavy crackdowns by Pakistani security forces. According to sources, Pakistani forces used lethal force against Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) during their long march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad.The crackdown reportedly resulted in the deaths of 20 civilians and left over 33 protesters injured.Amnesty International USA said that the disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot were consistent with Pakistani authorities’ “long history of unlawful violence against protesters”. “We urge the Pakistani authorities torestore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area,” it said.While security forces continue to maintain a heightened presence in Rawalakot, Muzaffarabad and other areas, sources said the possibility of additional protests remains high over the coming days because of declining public confidence in the political process.Local authorities have also continued to impose communication blackouts and suspended services across POK.
Article Summary: Pakistani forces used lethal force against Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) during their long march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad. The crackdown reportedly resulted in the deaths of 20 civilians and left over 33 protesters injured. Local authorities have also continued to impose communication blackouts and suspended services across POK.
