Article Title: Ex-PM Imran Khan's sister charged under cybercrime law over remarks on Pakistan army, India conflict
Article Text: NEW DELHI: Pakistan's anti-cybercrime agency has registered an FIR against Noreen Niazi, sister of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan , over remarks about the Pakistan military and last year's four-day conflict with India, an official said on Wednesday.The case was registered by the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA) in Islamabad under Sections 20 and 26-A of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA), nearly 10 days after the agency summoned Niazi for questioning over social media content it described as "false, offensive and inflammatory"."NCCIA in Islamabad has registered a case against Noreen Niazi, the sister of former prime minister Imran Khan, under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act (PECA)," an official told PTI.According to the FIR, Niazi made false and baseless allegations against Pakistan and its armed forces."Noreen Niazi attempted to undermine public confidence in the state and create panic among the people. She disseminated false, provocative, insulting and threatening content and conducted a systematic propaganda campaign against state and security institutions," the FIR said.The case stems from an interview that was widely circulated on social media, in which Niazi claimed the May 2025 India-Pakistan military confrontation was the result of collusion between Pakistan's military leadership and Prime Minister Narendra Modi and was orchestrated to enhance the image of Pakistan's armed forces.She also questioned Pakistan's military response during the four-day conflict that followed the Pahalgam terror attack and claimed, without providing evidence, that India deliberately refrained from escalating the conflict because Pakistan was moving towards recognising Israel and that the episode was intended to facilitate Islamabad's entry into the Abraham Accords."What do you think? ... India, which is a big country, was not in position to respond to Pakistan when it attacked on May 10?" Niazi said in the interview. "It could have but India deliberately refrained from giving a strong response because of some understanding."Pakistan's NCCIA had issued summons to Niazi on July 18, directing her to appear before investigators to record her statement in connection with the inquiry.
Article Summary: Pakistan's anti-cybercrime agency has registered an FIR against Noreen Niazi, sister of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan. The case stems from an interview that was widely circulated on social media, in which she claimed the May 2025 India-Pakistan military confrontation was the result of collusion between Pakistan's military leadership.

Article Title: 'They're enemies like India': Pakistan minister Khawaja Asif justifies killing of over 30 protesters in PoK
Article Text:
"I put the protesters of PojK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Khawaja Asif said.

Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif said he considered protesters in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK) enemies, just as he considered India."I put the protesters of PojK in the same category as India and consider them as enemies," Khawaja Asif said when asked about the protest that intensified on Monday leading to the killing of over 30 protesters.Moreover, the Amnesty International USA called the Pakistani crackdown on protestors as "disturbing" and urged Islamabad to "restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area.""The disturbing reports emerging from Rawalakot are consistent with the Pakistani authorities’ long history of unlawful violence against protesters in PoJK. We urge the Pakistani authorities to restore all communications access and allow media and independent observers into the area," Amnesty International USA posted on X.The protest erupted as thousands of demonstrators began marching towards Muzaffarabad after negotiations between the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) and the authorities broke down, while election officials postponed legislative assembly polls in two districts amid the unrest.The political crisis unfolded alongside the first phase of polling in 13 constituencies of the Mirpur division. However, political parties said the prolonged demonstrations had severely affected electioneering across the region.Campaign rallies, public meetings and door-to-door outreach have reportedly been disrupted by strikes and sit-ins, while candidates have expressed uncertainty over voter participation if the protests continue.Residents told local media that public interest in the elections had sharply declined, with many believing that longstanding grievances and basic rights should be addressed before any electoral exercise. According to several residents, enthusiasm for the polls is "almost non-existent," with the protest movement taking precedence over electoral politics.The ongoing agitation follows weeks of growing tensions in the region. On June 30, the JAAC criticised Pakistani authorities after an opposition delegation was reportedly prevented from entering PoJK, calling it another example of restrictions on democratic rights and political dissent.The committee also alleged that authorities had obstructed food supplies and curtailed access to the region, claims it said reflected the government's approach towards the people of PoJK.
Article Summary: Pakistan defence minister Khawaja Asif said he considered protesters in Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir (PoJK) enemies, just as he considered India. Amnesty International USA called the Pakistani crackdown on protestors as "disturbing" and urged Islamabad to "restore all communications access"

Article Title: PoK protests: Thousands march to Muzaffarabad after failed talks; polls delayed in two districts
Article Text:
Thousands march to Muzaffarabad after failed talks; polls delayed in two districts

Talks collapse, protesters hit the streets

Elections overshadowed by unrest

Protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) intensified on Monday as thousands of demonstrators began marching towards Muzaffarabad after negotiations between the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) and the authorities broke down, while election officials postponed legislative assembly polls in two districts amid the unrest.The Election Commission deferred voting in the Sudhnoti and Rawalakot constituencies until August 10, citing an ongoing sit-in led by the Public Action Committee (PAC).The postponement comes as a weeks-long protest movement continues to disrupt public life and cast uncertainty over the electoral process.The latest escalation followed the collapse of talks between JAAC leaders and the government on Saturday. Protest organisers alleged that authorities refused to release detained activists, withdraw criminal cases against protesters or agree to the committee's core demands.After the negotiations failed, JAAC issued an ultimatum, asking the government to formally notify acceptance of its demands by 1pm on July 27. It warned that if no action was taken, thousands of supporters would march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad — a call that was subsequently carried out.The demonstrations mark the latest phase of a protest campaign that has entered its 52nd day.The political crisis unfolded alongside the first phase of polling in 13 constituencies of the Mirpur division. However, political parties said the prolonged demonstrations had severely affected electioneering across the region.Campaign rallies, public meetings and door-to-door outreach have reportedly been disrupted by strikes and sit-ins, while candidates have expressed uncertainty over voter participation if the protests continue.Residents told local media that public interest in the elections had sharply declined, with many believing that longstanding grievances and basic rights should be addressed before any electoral exercise. According to several residents, enthusiasm for the polls is "almost non-existent," with the protest movement taking precedence over electoral politics.The ongoing agitation follows weeks of growing tensions in the region. On June 30, the JAAC criticised Pakistani authorities after an opposition delegation was reportedly prevented from entering PoK, calling it another example of restrictions on democratic rights and political dissent.The committee also alleged that authorities had obstructed food supplies and curtailed access to the region, claims it said reflected the government's approach towards the people of PoK.Meanwhile, Amnesty International has criticised Pakistan's handling of the situation ahead of the regional elections, accusing the authorities of using heavy-handed measures to suppress peaceful political dissent and violate fundamental human rights.
Article Summary: Thousands march to Muzaffarabad after failed talks; polls delayed in two districts. Election Commission deferred voting in the Sudhnoti and Rawalakot constituencies until August 10, citing an ongoing sit-in led by the Public Action Committee (PAC)

Article Title: Saudi money, Chinese weapons, American patronage: Can Pakistan balance all three?
Article Text:
Saudi Arabia Crown Prince and Prime Minister Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud (MBS), Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir Ahmed Shah, US President Donald Trump, President Xi Jinping.

Pakistan's foreign policy paradox: Punching above its weight while struggling at home

Mediating between Iran and the United States;

Deepening defence ties with Saudi Arabia;

Maintaining its strategic partnership with China;

Rebuilding relations with Donald Trump 's administration; and

's administration; and Coordinating closely with Turkey and Egypt on regional security issues.

How Saudi Arabia reportedly sought Pakistan's military support





Munir's attempt to redefine Pakistan's global role





China, Saudi Arabia and US: The three pillars of Pakistan's diplomacy





Rebuilding ties with Washington under Trump





Pakistan's role as mediator between Washington and Tehran





Growing security cooperation with Saudi Arabia





Balancing act comes with growing risks





Domestic troubles threaten Pakistan's global ambitions





Munir's 'hard state' vision





Economic fragility limits strategic ambitions





NEW DELHI: Pakistan is attempting one of its most ambitious foreign policy balancing acts in decades, seeking to simultaneously preserve its strategic partnership with China, deepen security ties with Saudi Arabia, rebuild relations with US President Donald Trump 's administration, mediate between Washington and Tehran, and strengthen coordination with Turkey and Egypt, according to a detailed Financial Times report.The report says Pakistan's military leadership under Field Marshal Asim Munir believes the country's geopolitical location and longstanding relationships across competing power centres have created a rare opportunity to elevate Islamabad's diplomatic profile despite mounting economic and security challenges at home.According to the report, Pakistan's efforts have become particularly visible during the recent Middle East crisis, with Islamabad attempting to position itself as a regional mediator while simultaneously expanding defence cooperation with Gulf monarchies and maintaining its decades-old strategic partnership with Beijing.However, analysts quoted by the newspaper warn that Pakistan's expanding diplomatic ambitions are unfolding against the backdrop of a fragile economy, worsening militancy and growing political repression, raising questions about whether Islamabad can sustain such an ambitious foreign policy.According to the report, Pakistan today finds itself pursuing an unusually complex foreign policy that requires it to balance sometimes competing strategic relationships.The newspaper says Islamabad is simultaneously:Former Pakistani brigadier Feroz Khan, quoted by the FT, says Pakistan has increasingly relied on diplomacy and military influence to compensate for its domestic weaknesses."Given its deep economic and political weaknesses, [Pakistan's] nuclear bomb, its conventional military forces and diplomacy are all it has to punch above its weight as a middle power," says Khan, who now teaches at the Naval Postgraduate School in California.According to the newspaper, Pakistan's military establishment believes the Middle East offers Islamabad greater strategic space than South Asia, where India's economic and military strength limits Pakistan's regional influence."As a south Asian power, Pakistan is permanently number two to India, the wealthier, stronger and more useful nation to the US in that region," Khan says. "But in the Middle East, it believes it can come into its own, with the blessing of US Central Command and Saudi Arabia."The report says Islamabad's diplomatic outreach has coincided with efforts by Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Turkey to play larger roles in shaping the region's post-war security architecture.According to analysts cited by the newspaper, this emerging grouping could eventually serve as a counterweight to growing military cooperation involving the United Arab Emirates, Israel and India.According to FT, one of the clearest illustrations of Pakistan's growing role came shortly before Islamabad hosted talks involving the United States and Iran earlier this year.The newspaper reports that on April 10, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed al-Jadaan visited Islamabad and met Pakistan's military chief Field Marshal Asim Munir at the Prime Minister House.Citing two people briefed on the discussions, FT says Saudi Arabia requested Pakistan's military support as the kingdom came under missile and drone attacks allegedly launched by Iran.According to the report, Riyadh had already signed a mutual defence agreement with Islamabad in 2025 and wanted Pakistan to provide personnel and military equipment.The newspaper says Pakistan's leadership was initially reluctant because such a move could complicate its planned mediation efforts between Washington and Tehran and trigger domestic political criticism from sections of Pakistan's population sympathetic to Iran.However, according to the report, Pakistan was also under severe financial pressure.The report says that only days earlier, the United Arab Emirates had unexpectedly demanded repayment of $3.5 billion in loans, equivalent to roughly one-fifth of Pakistan's foreign exchange reserves at the time.According to the newspaper, Pakistan eventually agreed to Saudi Arabia's request.The FT, citing people familiar with the matter, reports that Munir dispatched a squadron of fighter aircraft, air force personnel and a Chinese-made HQ-9 air defence system to a Saudi military base overlooking Iran's coastline.The report further claims that Saudi Arabia extended a $3 billion loan to Pakistan the following week.Pakistan's military spokesperson Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry rejected any suggestion that the deployment and the loan were linked."This is a special, decades-old relationship based on a very strong religious foundation and mutual respect," Chaudhry told the FT.The Saudi episode reflects a broader effort by Field Marshal Asim Munir to reshape Pakistan's international standing.According to the newspaper, Munir has sought to leverage Pakistan's longstanding relationships with China, Saudi Arabia and the United States while simultaneously presenting Islamabad as a credible diplomatic intermediary in regional crises.The report says Munir hopes to transform Pakistan into what he calls a "hard state" capable of restoring internal stability, defeating militancy, attracting foreign investment and projecting greater influence abroad.One former US diplomat who dealt extensively with Munir told the FT that the army chief "rules Pakistan with a 'massive chip on his shoulder'" and is determined to strengthen the country's security apparatus."Munir aspires to turn Pakistan into what he calls a 'hard state' and rules Pakistan with a 'massive chip on his shoulder'," the former diplomat said.According to the newspaper, Munir has increasingly concentrated power within Pakistan's military establishment since becoming army chief in November 2022.The Pakistan's parliament has granted him expanded authority, including extending his tenure and giving him greater oversight over the armed forces while critics accuse the government of weakening judicial independence and restricting political dissent.Analysts quoted by the newspaper argue that Munir believes tighter military control is necessary to restore order after years of political instability and economic decline.Yet, according to the report, Pakistan's growing diplomatic activism abroad contrasts sharply with the challenges confronting the country at home, including rising militant violence, slowing investment, mounting debt and increasing dependence on external financial assistance.According to the FT, Pakistan's current foreign policy rests on maintaining close ties with three major powers whose interests often diverge: China, Saudi Arabia and the United States.The newspaper says Beijing remains Islamabad's largest defence supplier and one of its most important strategic partners, while Saudi Arabia has become Pakistan's principal financial backer. At the same time, Pakistan has worked to rebuild ties with Washington under US President Donald Trump, despite decades of fluctuating relations.Pakistan military spokesperson Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry told the Financial Times that Islamabad's relationships with Beijing and Riyadh differ from conventional diplomatic partnerships."There are two countries with whom Pakistan has a special relationship: China and Saudi Arabia," Chaudhry said. "With them, there is never a quid pro quo."According to FT report, China has invested more than $30 billion in Pakistan through infrastructure, transport and power projects, including development of the strategically important Gwadar Port under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). Beijing has also played a central role in Pakistan's nuclear, missile and defence programmes over several decades and continues to be its largest supplier of military equipment.Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, remains Pakistan's biggest financial lifeline, according to the report. Besides repeated loans and deferred payment facilities, Riyadh has frequently rolled over debt repayments to help Islamabad avoid a balance-of-payments crisis.The Pakistan currently owes Saudi Arabia around $8 billion, equivalent to nearly 46 per cent of the country's central bank reserves, making the Gulf kingdom one of Islamabad's most important creditors.The FT report says Pakistan has also sought to restore relations with the United States after years of strained ties.According to the newspaper, Islamabad nominated Donald Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize in June last year for what it described as his "decisive diplomatic intervention" during Pakistan's brief military conflict with India.The report notes that Trump, who had once accused Pakistan of giving the United States "nothing but lies and deceit", has since publicly referred to Asim Munir as his "favourite field marshal", reflecting what the newspaper describes as one of the warmest periods in US-Pakistan relations in recent years.Accroding to the report, Washington also gave Pakistan greater diplomatic space during the recent Middle East crisis.Asfandyar Mir, senior fellow for South Asia at the Stimson Center in Washington, told the newspaper Munir had taken a considerable political gamble by placing Pakistan at the centre of diplomatic efforts."Munir took a significant risk by staking his standing on diplomacy that could easily have backfired," Mir said."But Trump, in a departure from the India-centric consensus that has defined American policy for a decade, allowed Pakistan to make its play."According to the report, Pakistan viewed improved ties with Washington as essential not only for regional diplomacy but also for maintaining access to Western financial institutions at a time when the country's economy remains heavily dependent on IMF support.According to the Financial Times, Pakistan attempted to use its relationships with both Iran and the United States to position itself as a neutral intermediary during the recent conflict.The newspaper reports that Asim Munir chaired marathon discussions between US Vice President JD Vance and Iranian representatives that eventually laid the groundwork for what the report describes as the "Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding", a 14-point ceasefire agreement.However, according to the Financial Times, those diplomatic gains proved short-lived after President Trump later declared the ceasefire "over" following renewed Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and authorised fresh military strikes.The newspaper says Tehran responded with missile and drone attacks against Gulf states while once again disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route through which most of Pakistan's imported oil passes.Despite the renewed conflict, Pakistan's military insists Islamabad continues to pursue diplomacy."Pakistan has a clear interest in peace in the larger Muslim world, and particularly the Gulf," Chaudhry told the Financial Times. "The countries of the Gulf know this and are therefore more comfortable dealing with us as a security partner and honest broker."The military spokesperson also said Pakistan had remained engaged with all major regional stakeholders."Pakistan has been working with all of the stakeholders in the Gulf as well as Iran to ensure that this war should not spiral and should not expand," Chaudhry said.The Financial Times says Pakistan's mediation efforts have coincided with rapidly expanding military cooperation with Saudi Arabia.According to the report, the two countries signed a mutual defence agreement in September 2025 that has not been made public but was approved without parliamentary debate.The newspaper says official statements from both governments described the agreement as stating that "any aggression against either country shall be considered an aggression against both."According to a person briefed on the discussions, cited by the Financial Times, Islamabad and Riyadh are also exploring the creation of a joint aerial defence system following vulnerabilities exposed during attacks on Saudi infrastructure.The newspaper says closer defence cooperation also serves Pakistan's own economic interests.More than 5.5 million Pakistanis work across Gulf countries, sending home over $20 billion annually in remittances that remain one of Pakistan's largest sources of foreign exchange.Umer Karim of the Riyadh-based King Faisal Centre for Research and Islamic Studies told the Financial Times that Saudi Arabia has repeatedly acted as Pakistan's financial backstop."In Saudi Arabia, you have a state which will always at least try to provide you with a degree of financial cushion in moments of great need," Karim said.The Financial Times says Pakistan's increasingly close relationship with Saudi Arabia also exposes Islamabad to new strategic vulnerabilities.According to the report, Pakistan remains heavily dependent on Saudi financial assistance while also sharing deep religious, cultural and historical ties with neighbouring Iran.The newspaper notes that Pakistan is home to one of the world's largest Shia populations, estimated at around 40 million, making any perceived tilt towards Riyadh politically sensitive.According to the Financial Times, tensions became particularly evident after the assassination of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei earlier this year, which reportedly triggered riots in several Pakistani cities that left at least two dozen people dead.The report also says Pakistan faced additional financial pressure when the United Arab Emirates demanded immediate repayment of $3.5 billion in loans, reflecting what analysts describe as growing geopolitical competition within the Gulf.Karim warned that Pakistan's dependence on Saudi Arabia could eventually leave it with limited diplomatic flexibility."Considering Pakistan's indispensable financial dependence on Saudi Arabia, it essentially won't have much of a choice," he told the Financial Times.The newspaper concludes that Pakistan's attempt to simultaneously retain Chinese strategic support, Saudi financial backing and improved relations with Washington represents one of the most complex balancing acts in its modern diplomatic history.However, analysts quoted throughout the report caution that sustaining such a strategy will ultimately depend on Islamabad's ability to stabilise its economy, improve internal security and reduce its dependence on foreign creditors.While Pakistan has attempted to expand its diplomatic influence abroad, the Financial Times says the country's domestic challenges remain severe and could ultimately limit Islamabad's ability to sustain its ambitious foreign policy.According to the newspaper, Pakistan's economy continues to struggle under mounting debt, repeated balance-of-payments crises and dependence on international lenders. The country of around 255 million people has received 25 IMF bailout programmes, while official poverty climbed to a decade high of 29 per cent last year.The Financial Times says Pakistan also continues to battle a deteriorating security environment. Security forces are fighting Baloch separatist groups and the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), both of which have intensified attacks in the country's western regions, disrupting plans to develop mineral-rich provinces and attract foreign investment.Critics quoted by the newspaper argue that Islamabad's growing diplomatic profile cannot compensate for deep-rooted domestic weaknesses."What good is a bigger voice on the world stage if the house is on fire?" former Pakistani ambassador to the United States and the United Kingdom Maleeha Lodhi told the Financial Times."Pakistan needs to fix the cracks within."According to the Financial Times, Field Marshal Asim Munir has sought to address Pakistan's internal instability by transforming the country into what he describes as a "hard state."The newspaper says Munir believes stronger military control is necessary to restore law and order, eliminate militancy, end years of political instability and create conditions for economic recovery.One former US diplomat who dealt extensively with Munir described the army chief's governing style in stark terms."Munir aspires to turn Pakistan into what he calls a 'hard state' and rules Pakistan with a 'massive chip on his shoulder'," the former diplomat told the Financial Times.According to the report, Munir, who became Pakistan's army chief in November 2022, has steadily expanded the military's influence over civilian institutions.The Financial Times says Pakistan's parliament has extended his tenure, granted him greater authority over the armed forces and backed legislation that critics say has weakened judicial independence and curtailed public criticism of the military.The newspaper notes that Munir and his supporters blame years of civilian-led governments for Pakistan's political instability and economic decline.The Financial Times says Pakistan's diplomatic ambitions ultimately depend on economic strength that the country has yet to achieve.According to the World Bank data cited by the newspaper, Pakistan spends substantially less than comparable lower-middle-income countries on health and education, leaving around 25 million children out of school. Nearly 78 per cent of children are unable to read at the expected level by the age of 10, while around 40 per cent suffer from stunted growth.Although the IMF recently praised Pakistan's implementation of its $7 billion bailout programme, the Financial Times says the country's debt burden remains overwhelming.According to Fitch Ratings, interest payments alone are expected to consume around 40 per cent of government revenues by the financial year ending June 2027.The newspaper reports that Pakistan has also sought $10 billion in financial assistance from Washington to strengthen its foreign exchange reserves.Despite official projections of 3.7 per cent economic growth, Pakistan's trade deficit has widened to a four-year high of $39.6 billion, driven by weak exports, rising imports and higher global commodity prices linked to the conflict in the Gulf.Stefan Dercon, an Oxford professor advising Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on economic reforms, warned that policymakers recognise the urgency of the situation."There's a small group of decision makers... that realise if they don't fix this economy, they will fall off the cliff of a deep economic and even political crisis," he told the Financial Times.
Article Summary: Pakistan's foreign policy paradox: Punching above its weight while struggling at home. Mediating between Iran and the United States. Deepening defence ties with Saudi Arabia. Maintaining its strategic partnership with China.Rebuilding relations with Donald Trump's administration. Coordinating closely with Turkey and Egypt on regional security issues.

Article Title: Nirmal Purja — star climber, elite British officer & MBE — dead on PoK peak
Article Text:
Purja, who died five days after his 43rd birthday, had been attempting to become the first mountaineer to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice without supplemental oxygen

Nepal-born British mountaineer Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja, 43, died with nine other climbers after an avalanche struck the 8,047m Broad Peak in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) on July 30, only nine days after he became the first person to scale Gasherbrum II (8,035 metres) without supplemental oxygen. Elite Exped, the agency Purja co-founded, confirmed Saturday afternoon that all 10 members of the international team had died and there were no survivors, though authorities had not recovered all the bodies. Victims of the Karakoram tragedy included six Nepalese and one climber each from Pakistan, Oman, US and China.Purja, who died five days after his 43rd birthday, had been attempting to become the first mountaineer to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice without supplemental oxygen. The ascent of Gasherbrum II on July 21 marked his 57th ascent of an 8,000m peak and his 29th without bottled oxygen. He then made a last-minute decision to attempt nearby Broad Peak during the same PoK expedition.Born in Myagdi district in 1983 and raised in Chitwan — in Nepal’s plains — Purja later became a British citizen. He spent 16 years in the British military, serving with Brigade of Gurkhas before becoming the first Gurkha to join Special Boat Service, Royal Navy’s special forces unit.Queen Elizabeth II appointed him MBE in 2018.Purja began his climbing journey in 2012 with what was meant to be a trek to Everest Base Camp but pushed beyond the original plan and turned the hike into a summit attempt. The experience became an early lesson in ambition and endurance. He first summited Mount Everest in 2016 and returned to the summit five more times, the last ascent occurring earlier this year.The climber, mourned by mountaineers across the world, entered history books in 2019 by climbing all 14 peaks above 8,000m in six months and six days, smashing a record that had stood at nearly eight years. His extraordinary life was immortalised by the Netflix documentary ‘14 Peaks’. Purja would later complete all 14 without supplemental oxygen and joined the all-Nepalese team that made K2’s first winter ascent in Jan 2021.In a Facebook post days before his death, Purja wrote, “This was never the plan. Initially, the plan was to climb just G2,” adding that a successful Broad Peak ascent would leave only Cho Oyu in his record bid. He ended the post with a line that became poignant after the disaster: “Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted. Not one.”Purja had launched ‘Hat-Trick Project’ last year with the extraordinary aim of climbing all 14 eight-thousanders and Seven Summits three times each.The other Nepalese victims included Pur Bahadur Gurung, known as Yukta; Kili Pemba Sherpa, Nima Sherpa, Nawang Thindu Sherpa and Gyalu Sherpa. Omani climber Nadhira Ahmed Al Harthy, American Mallory Geis, Pakistani climber Sohail Sakhi and China’s Wang Zhong also died. Al Harthy was the first Omani woman to scale Everest, while Geis was attempting her first 8,000m peak in PoK. Sakhi, a geographer, guide and high-altitude photographer, was undertaking what was expected to be his final expedition.Purja and his team’s geo trackers showed climbers losing hundreds of metres in altitude before their signals stopped around 9am on Thursday. His tracker later appeared to change location, briefly raising hopes that he might have survived. Search teams used drones to locate bodies as bad weather and avalanche danger hampered operations.Paying tribute, Nepal PM Balendra Shah said, “The Himalayas grant the glory of the peak to many, and sometimes hold them forever in their embrace,” adding that Purja and the other climbers would remain immortal through their bravery and contribution.Reinhold Messner, the legendary Italian alpinist widely regarded as one of the greatest high-altitude climbers in history, also paid tribute to Purja. Now 81, Messner, who was the first person to summit all 14 eight-thousanders without supplementary oxygen and helped establish the minimalist alpine style in the Himalayas, said, “Nims chose his own path with courage and passion. What remains is not only the sorrow of his passing, but the memory of a life truly lived. My thoughts are with his family, his friends, and everyone who had the privilege of knowing him.”------------------Nimsdai’s Record Trail-----------------------Summited all 14 8-thousanders in 189 days in 2019All 8-thousanders without supplemental oxygen in 2 years, 5 months in 2024First to summit K2 in winter in Jan 2021Everest, Lhotse, Makalu in 2 days, 30 minutes57 successful 8-thousander ascents29 8-thousander ascents without supplemental oxygenFirst Gurkha to serve with UK’s Special Boat ServiceMBE for services to high-altitude mountaineering in 2018
Article Summary: Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja, 43, died with nine other climbers after an avalanche struck the 8,047m Broad Peak in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir. Victims of the Karakoram tragedy included six Nepalese and one climber each from Pakistan, Oman, US and China. He had been attempting to become the first mountaineer to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice without supplemental oxygen.

Article Title: Mountaineer Nirmal Purja killed in avalanche on PoK peak, says his company
Article Text:
Nepalese mountaineering icon Nirmal Purja (file photo) has been confirmed dead after an avalanche on Broad Peak

Nirmal “Nims Dai” Purja, the legendary Nepal-born mountaineer who climbed all 14 of the world’s 8,000-metre peaks in a record six months and six days, has been confirmed dead after an avalanche struck his expedition on PoK’s Broad Peak.Purja, 43, was confirmed dead on Saturday by his expedition company Elite Exped, ending a two-day search operation after the avalanche swept a group of climbers down the 8,047-metre mountain on Thursday.“It is with profound sadness and immense heartbreak that we confirm that Nirmal ‘Nimsdai’ Purja tragically lost his life following the avalanche on Broad Peak,” Elite Exped said in a statement.The company also confirmed the deaths of Purja’s climbing partners and guides, Pur Bahadur Gurung, known as “Yukta”, and Nima Sherpa. Other members of the expedition were also killed in the avalanche.Nepal PM Balendra Shah paid tribute to Purja and his fellow climbers climbers killed on Broad Peak. In a post, Shah said mountaineering was not merely about reaching a summit but represented “courage, discipline, sacrifice and the indomitable confidence to challenge human limits”. He said the climbers’ courage and dedication would remain an enduring source of inspiration.He offered his condolences to the deceased climbers and expressed sympathy to their families, relatives and well-wishers.The avalanche struck on July 30 as the expedition climbed between Camp 2 and higher elevations on Broad Peak in PoK’s Karakoram range. The entire team lost communication after the avalanche, while rescue efforts were hampered by poor weather and the danger of further avalanches.Tracking data showed Purja at about 6,660 metres shortly before the avalanche. His device later indicated a sharp drop in altitude, suggesting he had been swept hundreds of metres down the mountain. The signal subsequently stopped.Military helicopters and ground teams led by experienced Nepali climbers joined the search. Rescuers located several of the missing climbers, but none showed signs of life. Recovery teams continued searching for the remaining missing climbers.Purja had been attempting to add Broad Peak to an already extraordinary climbing record. In 2019, he completed all 14 of the world's peaks above 8,000 metres in six months and six days as part of his Project Possible expedition, breaking the previous record of more than seven years.He later became the fastest climber to complete all 14 eight-thousanders without supplementary oxygen and was attempting to become the first person to climb all 14 twice without supplemental oxygen.A former British Gurkha and Special Boat Service soldier, Purja entered mountaineering after a 2012 trek to Everest Base Camp. His 2019 record-breaking expedition was later chronicled in the Netflix documentary “14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible”, bringing him international recognition.Purja was also part of the Nepali team that made the first winter ascent of K2 in January 2021. He later founded Elite Exped and the Nimsdai Foundation and became a prominent advocate for Nepali climbers and high-altitude workers.His death came days after he wrote on Instagram that he was seeking “nothing but safe passage” up and down Broad Peak, adding that he took no mountain for granted. His passing is a great loss to the mountaineering community and the people of Nepal.
Article Summary: Nepalese mountaineer Nirmal Purja has been confirmed dead after an avalanche on Broad Peak. The 43-year-old climbed all 14 of the world’s 8,000-metre peaks in a record six months and six days. Other members of the expedition were also killed in the avalanche.

Article Title: Nepal communal violence: Three killed, curfew widens; PM Balendra Shah appeals for calm
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view What is the best way to maintain peace during communal tensions? Dialogue and understanding Stronger security measures 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Nepal prime minister Balendra Shah on Thursday appealed for unity, restraint and social harmony after at least three people were killed in communal violence that began in Sunsari district and later spread to neighbouring Madhesh province. The violence prompted authorities to expand curfews and tighten security across several districts.Addressing the nation for the first time since the violence erupted, Shah said the government was treating the situation with its "full seriousness and sensitivity" and pledged a fair and transparent investigation into the clashes."The Government of Nepal is completely serious and sensitive about the tragic incident that took place in Dewanganj, Siraha and other places in Sunsari a few days ago and the turbulent atmosphere that has arisen in some districts since then," Shah said in the televised address.The government's response comes amid curfews, prohibitory orders and heightened security deployments in Sunsari, Siraha, Dhanusa and Parsa districts. Since Sunday, protests and tensions have spread across Nepal's southern plains, raising concerns over wider communal friction in areas bordering India.Violence spread to neighbouring Madhesh province on Thursday, where a teenager died during clashes in Golbazar market in Siraha district.Officials also confirmed that a person injured in the earlier violence in Sunsari succumbed to injuries in Koshi province, taking the death toll to three.According to officials, the unrest began late on Sunday in Ward No. 3 of Dewanganj rural municipality in Sunsari district after a dispute between local groups over loud music during preparations for the Bol Bam pilgrimage to the Saptakoshi River. AFPreported that tensions escalated over loud music and religious flags during a Hindu procession, prompting police to open fire to disperse the crowd, according to local official Poshan Lamichhane.The confrontation escalated into stone-pelting and violence, prompting police to intervene with batons, tear gas, warning shots and eventually live fire by the Armed Police Force. One person died on the spot from gunshot injuries, while several others were critically injured.Shah announced that the ministry of home affairs had formed an investigation committee and assured the public that those responsible would be prosecuted."As soon as the incident happened, all security agencies immediately reached the spot and made continuous efforts to normalise the situation, prevent further unpleasant incidents and maintain peace and security. The Ministry of Home Affairs has formed an investigation committee to conduct a fair investigation into the incident and take strict legal action against the culprits." he said.The prime minister said the government had adopted a multi-pronged approach to restore normalcy. He said an all-party meeting had been convened at the central level, while continuous dialogue was under way with local representatives, civil society members, religious leaders, community representatives and social activists."In addition, a meeting of the National Security Council has been convened to seriously review the overall peace and security situation in the country and necessary decisions have been taken according to the situation," Shah said.In his four-and-a-half-minute televised address, Shah also urged citizens not to circulate misinformation or inflammatory content that could worsen tensions." The essence of all religions is compassion, mercy, love and peace. Blaming an entire community for an unexpected and tragic incident in one part of the country and spreading the fire of revenge for it in other parts of the country cannot be justified or justified from any perspective," he said.Concluding his address in both Nepali and Maithili, Shah appealed for collective efforts to restore peace and preserve national unity."Our history is a witness that even in the most difficult and difficult situations, mutual unity, tolerance and conscience have become our greatest strength. We all have to play the role of responsible citizens and remove the clouds of unrest that have hung over this beautiful and peaceful Nepali sky. We, the common citizens, civil society, religious communities, all respected leaders, all political parties and responsible media, are making a heartfelt appeal to the government to exercise patience and restraint and maintain peace, harmony, brotherhood and national unity," he said.
Article Summary: Nepal's prime minister Balendra Shah appeals for unity, restraint and social harmony. Shah says the government is treating the situation with its "full seriousness and sensitivity" The violence prompted authorities to expand curfews and tighten security across several districts.

Article Title: 10 climbers, including Nirmal Purja, missing after avalanche on Broad Peak in PoK's Gilgit-Baltistan
Article Text:
Who is Nirmal Purja?

Four bodies have been recovered by Pakistani authorities out of the ten international climbers who had gone missing after an avalanche struck Broad Peak, one of the world's highest mountains in Pakistan-occupied Gilgit-Baltistan. The list of climbers includes world renowned Nepal-born mountaineer Nirmal Purja According to the Alpine Club of Pakistan, the avalanche hit the expedition around midday on Thursday on the 8,047-metre (26,400-foot) Broad Peak in the Karakoram range, the Associated Press reported.The team comprised of five Nepalese climbers, Pakistani mountaineer Sohail Sakhi from Hunza, Omani climber Nathira, American climber Mallory Geis, a Chinese climber identified only as Wang, and another foreign climber, the club said.The team has remained out of communication since the incident. However, a tracking device carried by Purja has continued to show movement, offering a glimmer of hope as rescuers race against time to reach the team.Speaking to Kantipur on Friday, Purja's business partner and Nepal lawmaker Mingma Gyabu Sherpa said data from the mountaineer's tracking device indicated that his location had changed after the avalanche."Initially, it appeared that he had been swept downhill by the avalanche," Sherpa was quoted as saying by The Kathmandu Post. "But after the point where the tracking had stopped, the location appears to have shifted again."Sherpa cautioned that the tracking data could not confirm Purja's condition but said it suggested some movement after the avalanche. He added that detailed information about the incident reached them only on Thursday evening, several hours after the avalanche struck.Poor weather has so far prevented helicopters from taking off, delaying aerial search-and-rescue operations. Sherpa said authorities were preparing to deploy helicopters on Friday morning if weather conditions improved.The club said it was working closely with government authorities to launch an immediate search-and-rescue operation. Its president, Maj Gen Irfan Arshad, and senior officials are coordinating efforts to mobilise helicopters and other rescue resources as soon as weather and operational conditions permit.Purja, also known as Nims Dai, is a Nepal-born British mountaineer and former Royal Marine. He joined the British Army in 2003 and became a Royal Marine in 2009.He rose to global prominence in 2019 after climbing all 14 of the world's 8,000-metre peaks in just 189 days, setting a record at the time.His achievement was later featured in the Netflix documentary "14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible." The record was surpassed in 2023 by a Norwegian climber and her Nepali Sherpa guide.Purja began his mountaineering career in 2012 after trekking to the Everest Base Camp. Instead of returning home as planned, he decided to climb Mount Everest , marking the start of his career as a high-altitude climber.
Article Summary: Four bodies have been recovered by Pakistani authorities out of the ten international climbers who had gone missing after an avalanche struck Broad Peak. The list of climbers includes world renowned Nepal-born mountaineer Nirmal Purja. A tracking device carried by Purja has continued to show movement, offering a glimmer of hope as rescuers race against time.

Article Title: Parliamentary committee seeks normalisation of visa operations in Bangladesh, govt says Hasina not allowed to undertake any political activity
Article Text:
Parl committee seeks normalisation of visa operations in Bangladesh, govt says Hasina not allowed to undertake any political activity

A Parliamentary committee on external affairs expressed concern that reduced visa processing volumes for Bangladesh nationals and security-related disruptions may adversely affect public perception and impede people-to-people engagement, which is vital for fostering bilateral ties.The Committee also noted the government's position that while providing refuge to former PM Sheikh Hasina , it had strictly adhered to the principle that no political activity is directed against any other country from Indian territory. The committee was informed by the government that it does not provide her with a political platform or any space to undertake any political activity from Indian territory.Recognizing the importance of sustained inter-personal contact for preserving mutual trust and confidence, the committee urged that the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) to work with security agencies and progressively normalize visa operations in Bangladesh "as soon as the situation permits"It also urged the ministry to develop a bilateral consular cooperation mechanism to periodically review visa policy, address grievances, and ensure that legitimate travellers are not subjected to various inconveniences, while maintaining necessary security safeguards. These recommendations were included in the Action Taken by the Government on the Observations/ Recommendations contained in the Ninth Report of the Committee on the subject ‘Future of India-Bangladesh Relationship’.Following the events of 5 August, 2024, that led to Hasina's exit, visa services were significantly scaled down, and consular personnel were withdrawn from Bangladesh. The MEA told the committee that1,500 visas are currently being issued each day across five centers in Bangladesh with medical visas accounting for approximately 80% of the total visas issued."The evolving security situation is under continuous review, and any decision on increasing daily issuance of visas or operationalizing additional visa centers will be taken in coordination with the relevant ministries of the government of India," it said.On the Hasina issue, the committee noted that the stay of Hasina in the country and India’s approach in this regard is guided by its civilizational ethos and humanitarian tradition of offering refuge to individuals facing circumstances of grave distress or existential threat.Taking note also of Dhaka's request for her extradition, the committee recommended that the government continue to uphold its principled and humanitarian approach, consistent with India’s "values and international responsibilities, while ensuring that such situations are managed with due sensitivity".
Article Summary: A Parliamentary committee on external affairs expressed concern that reduced visa processing volumes for Bangladesh nationals may adversely affect public perception. The Committee also noted the government's position that while providing refuge to former PM Sheikh Hasina, it had strictly adhered to the principle that no political activity is directed against any other country.
